claim: In the 'double-drift' illusion, local motion within a window moving in the periphery of the visual field alters the window's perceived path.
source: In the 'double-drift' illusion, local motion within a window moving in the periphery of the visual field alters the window's perceived path.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the double-drift illusion that is established in the literature and forms the basis of the study.

claim: The double-drift illusion is strong even when the eyes track a target whose motion matches the window so that the stimulus remains stable on the retina.
source: The illusion is strong even when the eyes track a target whose motion matches the window so that the stimulus remains stable on the retina.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about the double-drift illusion during smooth pursuit.

claim: The double-drift illusion during smooth pursuit implies that the illusion involves the integration of retinal signals with non-retinal eye-movement signals.
source: This implies that the illusion involves the integration of retinal signals with non-retinal eye-movement signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the illusion persists when the stimulus is retinally stabilized.

claim: Multiple cortical areas responded more strongly during the illusion than a control condition that was matched for low-level stimulus properties.
source: We identified a number of cortical areas that responded more strongly during the illusion than a control condition that was matched for low-level stimulus properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data comparing illusion and control conditions.

claim: Only in area hMT+ was it possible to decode the illusory trajectory.
source: Only in area hMT+ was it possible to decode the illusory trajectory.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the main experimental finding based on multivariate decoding analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Subjects accurately tracked the moving target during fMRI scanning.
source: Concurrent eye tracking confirmed that subjects accurately tracked the moving target
evidence: This is supported by concurrent eye tracking measurements during fMRI.

claim: The illusion trajectory could not be decoded using eye position measurements recorded during fMRI scanning.
source: we were unable to decode the illusion trajectory using eye position measurements recorded during fMRI scanning, ruling out explanations based on differences in oculomotor behavior.
evidence: This is based on decoding analysis applied to eye tracking data collected during fMRI.

claim: The results provide evidence for a perceptual representation in human visual cortex that incorporates extraretinal information.
source: Our results provide evidence for a perceptual representation in human visual cortex that incorporates extraretinal information.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons throughout visual cortex encode the location of visual stimuli on the retina.
source: Neurons throughout visual cortex encode the location of visual stimuli on the retina, suggesting that the visual system uses a primarily retina-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the neuroscience literature about visual cortex organization.

claim: Visual perception is stable across frequent eye movements that displace the retinal image.
source: Yet visual perception is stable across frequent eye movements that displace the retinal image.
evidence: This is a well-established observation in visual neuroscience.

claim: Neurons in the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) in macaque monkeys exhibit receptive fields that do not change position when the eyes move.
source: This idea has perhaps received its strongest support from monkey single-unit recording studies showing that neurons in the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) in macaque monkeys exhibit receptive fields that do not change position when the eyes move (Duhamel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Visually evoked responses in both human MT/MST (hMT+) and the lateral occipital complex (LOC) have been reported to be invariant to changes in eye position.
source: For example, visually evoked responses in both human MT/MST (hMT+) and the lateral occipital complex (LOC) have been reported to be invariant to changes in eye position (d'Avossa et al., 2007; McKyton and Zohary, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: A number of studies have measured spatial receptive fields for a range of eye positions and found that receptive fields change position when the eyes move.
source: For example, a number of studies have measured spatial receptive fields for a range of eye positions and found that receptive fields change position when the eyes move, suggesting that the brain uses a retinotopic reference frame (Gardner et al., 2008; Golomb and Kanwisher, 2012; Merriam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The reference frame of visual responses can shift from retinotopic to spatiotopic depending on the attentional state of the observer.
source: For example, Crespi et al., 2011 reported that the reference frame of visual responses can shift from retinotopic to spatiotopic depending on the attentional state of the observer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Spatiotopic representations become more prominent in tasks requiring sequences of eye movements.
source: Behavioral studies have reported that spatiotopic representations become more prominent in tasks requiring sequences of eye movements, suggesting that spatiotopic coordinates are built-up over time (Poletti et al., 2013; Sun and Goldberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific behavioral studies.

claim: The double-drift illusion occurs when a combination of local motion and an orthogonal global motion trajectory causes a strong perception of illusory drift away from the veridical trajectory.
source: The double-drift illusion occurs when a combination of local motion and an orthogonal global motion trajectory causes a strong perception of illusory drift away from the veridical trajectory.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the double-drift illusion based on established literature.

claim: The double-drift illusion can be strikingly large so that the stimulus appears to deviate by as much as 45° away from the veridical motion path.
source: The illusion can be strikingly large so that the stimulus appears to deviate by as much as 45° away from the veridical motion path (Tse and Hsieh, 2006; Shapiro et al., 2010; Lisi and Cavanagh, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies characterizing the illusion magnitude.

claim: The double-drift illusion persists even during smooth pursuit when the stimulus is stabilized on the retina.
source: A recent study revealed that the illusion persists even during smooth pursuit when the stimulus is stabilized on the retina (Cavanagh and Tse, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Several brain areas encode stable stimulus position during pursuit eye movements.
source: A number of brain areas encode stable stimulus position during pursuit eye movements (i.e., 'real position' cells) (Nau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: When subjects were attending to a task at fixation, the illusion could still be decoded from activity in LO, V3A/B, and hMT+, but not from EVC.
source: When subjects were attending to a task at fixation (Exp 2), the illusion could still be decoded from activity in LO, V3A/B, and hMT+, but not from EVC.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from Experiment 2 with the fixation task.

claim: Overall decoding accuracy was slightly reduced when participants performed a demanding task at fixation.
source: While overall decoding accuracy was slightly reduced in this experiment, we found that decoding accuracy remained robust and significant in LO, hMT+, and V3A/B, but not in early visual cortex (EVC) (Figure 3A, right)
evidence: This is based on comparison of decoding results between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.

claim: The classifier was sensitive to information related to encoding the perceived position of the stimulus during the illusion.
source: Instead, we conclude that the classifier was sensitive to information related to encoding the perceived position of the stimulus during the illusion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing decoding persists when attention is controlled.

claim: Only area hMT+ could discriminate leftward from rightward illusory paths.
source: Of all the visual areas tested, only area hMT+ could discriminate leftward from rightward illusory paths (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from trajectory decoding analysis.

claim: The ability to discriminate the illusory motion path suggests a non-retinotopic representation of stimulus position.
source: Because the stimulus remained at a constant retinal location, the ability to discriminate the illusory motion path suggests a non-retinotopic representation of stimulus position.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental finding that trajectory can be decoded despite constant retinal position.

claim: Voxels that responded in the pursuit localizer do not carry information that distinguishes the drift paths in any of the ROIs.
source: We found that responses in these voxels do not carry information that distinguishes the drift paths, in any of the ROIs (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is based on decoding analysis using voxels selective for pursuit eye movements.

claim: The information being utilized by the classifier is not due to differences in pursuit eye movements.
source: Results from this control analysis suggest that the information being utilized by the classifier is not due to differences in pursuit eye movements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control analysis using pursuit-selective voxels.

claim: There was no information contained in the oculomotor behavior related to perceiving the illusion.
source: In this subset of subjects, we replicated our main fMRI results (decoding the illusion trajectory from hMT+ responses), but we were unable to decode the illusory trajectory from the eye position measurements alone, indicating that there was no information contained in the oculomotor behavior related to perceiving the illusion (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on decoding analysis applied to concurrent eye tracking data.

claim: There were no reliable differences in microsaccade characteristics (amplitude and direction) between illusory conditions.
source: Moreover, we quantified microsaccade characteristics (amplitude and direction) and found no reliable differences between illusory conditions (illusion vs. no-illusion), or between the direction of the illusion (left vs. right).
evidence: This is based on analysis of microsaccade data from eye tracking.

claim: Oculomotor behavior was unlikely an underlying cause of the fMRI findings.
source: We conclude that oculomotor behavior was unlikely an underlying cause of the fMRI findings reported here.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eye tracking control analyses.

claim: The classifier was unable to decode the conditions containing local motion alone.
source: However, the classifier was unable to decode the conditions containing local motion alone (i.e., discriminating left-followed-by-right from right-followed-by-leftward; Figure 3C, right).
evidence: This is based on decoding analysis of the local motion control conditions in Experiment 3.

claim: Information about illusory motion paths in hMT+ is not due to local motion of the stimulus alone.
source: This result demonstrates that information about illusory motion paths in hMT+ is not due to local motion of the stimulus alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the local motion control experiment results.

claim: fMRI BOLD responses in several visual cortical areas could reliably discriminate the double-drift illusion from a control condition that was matched for motion energy.
source: We found that fMRI BOLD responses in several visual cortical areas could reliably discriminate the double-drift illusion from a control condition that was matched for motion energy.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental findings.

claim: In EVC, decoding of the illusion could be explained by attentional effects associated with perceiving the illusion.
source: In EVC, this result could be explained by attentional effects associated with perceiving the illusion, since when attention was directed away from the illusion, decoding in EVC dropped to chance.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing results between attend-stimulus and attend-fixation conditions.

claim: Responses in hMT+ could discriminate the illusory drift path, suggesting that retinal and extraretinal information are integrated in hMT+.
source: Moreover, responses in hMT+ could also discriminate the illusory drift path, suggesting that retinal and extraretinal information are integrated in hMT+ and used to construct the spatiotopic perception experienced during the illusion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trajectory decoding results in hMT+.

claim: Non-retinal stimulus position encoding occurs in human extrastriate visual cortex.
source: Our results may indicate non-retinal stimulus position encoding occurs in human extrastriate visual cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the overall pattern of results.

claim: A coarse-scale map for direction of motion has been observed throughout visual cortex, including all of the areas included in the study.
source: One possibility is related to a coarse-scale map for direction of motion, which has been observed throughout visual cortex, including all of the areas included in our study (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The coarse-scale map for direction of motion in early visual areas (V1/V2/V3) is thought to result from an aperture-inward bias.
source: The coarse-scale map for direction of motion in early visual areas (V1/V2/V3) is thought to result from an aperture-inward bias: larger responses were observed for motion away from the aperture edge (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The coarse-scale map observed in hMT+ consisted of a bias for motion toward the fovea.
source: In contrast, the coarse-scale map observed in hMT+ did not depend on the aperture boundary, but instead consisted of a bias for motion toward the fovea (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: A net motion bias toward the fovea in hMT+ is unlikely to account for the observed results.
source: We think it is hence unlikely that a net motion bias toward the fovea in hMT + accounts for the observed results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the balanced design of the experimental conditions.

claim: Differences in BOLD activity to the two illusory drift paths arise because of the topographic organization within hMT+.
source: An alternative account is that differences in BOLD activity to the two illusory drift paths arise because of the topographic organization within hMT+ (Huk et al., 2002; Amano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The average eccentricity of the perceived drift path is higher during rightward drift and lower during leftward drift.
source: Thus, the average eccentricity of the perceived drift path is higher during rightward drift and lower during leftward drift.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometry of the illusory trajectories.

claim: There is an explicit representation of the perceived position of a stimulus in hMT+, while position encoding in EVC is entirely veridical.
source: This second account depends on there being an explicit representation of the perceived position of a stimulus in hMT+, while position encoding in EVC is entirely veridical.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential decoding results across brain areas.

claim: BOLD activity in hMT+ reflects the illusory position during motion-induced position shift.
source: Consistent with this account, one fMRI study (Maus et al., 2013) has reported that BOLD activity in hMT+ reflects the illusory position during motion-induced position shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Activity throughout visual cortex is known to encode stimulus position in retinal, not spatiotopic, coordinates.
source: Activity throughout visual cortex is known to encode stimulus position in retinal, not spatiotopic, coordinates (Gardner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: It remains unknown whether retinotopic coding is also universal in visual cortex for motion illusions.
source: However, it remains unknown whether retinotopic coding is also universal in visual cortex for motion illusions.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The data may imply a difference between EVC and downstream areas in the spatial encoding of illusory motion.
source: If the second account is accurate, our data may imply a difference between EVC and downstream areas in the spatial encoding of illusory motion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: In the smooth-pursuit variant of the illusion, the envelope only has a trajectory when defined in spatiotopic coordinates.
source: In the smooth-pursuit variant of the illusion, the envelope only has a trajectory when defined in spatiotopic coordinates, since the stimulus remains at a constant retinal location.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometry of the stimulus during smooth pursuit.

claim: The presence of the illusion with a stable position of the stimulus on the retina suggests some degree of spatiotopic processing in the brain.
source: With a stable position of the stimulus on the retina, the presence of the illusion suggests some degree of spatiotopic processing in the brain (Turi and Burr, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation.

claim: Spatiotopic processing could be accomplished by the formation of an explicit spatiotopic reference frame.
source: This could be accomplished by the formation of an explicit spatiotopic reference frame (Duhamel et al., 1997; d'd'Avossa et al., 2007; Crespi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative possibility supported by citations.

claim: Spatiotopic processing could be accomplished through a computation by which a retinotopic input is combined with an eye position gain field.
source: Alternatively this could be accomplished through a computation by which a retinotopic input is combined with an eye position gain field (Merriam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative possibility supported by citation.

claim: When subjects were attending the stimulus, illusion decoding was possible in all the visual areas studied.
source: When subjects were attending the stimulus, illusion decoding was possible in all the visual areas that we studied, raising the possibility that the illusion attracted attention, resulting in a higher BOLD response during illusory blocks (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental results from Experiment 1.

claim: The locus of attention can affect the apparent reference frame in which a stimulus is encoded.
source: Previous fMRI studies have claimed that the locus of attention can affect the apparent reference frame in which a stimulus is encoded (Crespi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Attention and task do have an impact on the spatial encoding of the double-drift illusion.
source: Our results in Exp 2, in which subjects attended fixation, and not the stimulus, demonstrate that attention and task do have an impact on the spatial encoding of the double-drift illusion
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results across experiments with different attentional demands.

claim: Both spatiotopic representations and receptive field remapping underlie visual stability across eye movements.
source: Behavioral investigations into mechanisms for visual stability across eye movements have found evidence that both spatiotopic representations and receptive field remapping underly visual stability (Poletti et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: After a single saccade, receptive field remapping is the primary mechanism underlying visual stability.
source: After a single saccade, receptive field remapping is the primary mechanism underlying visual stability, whereas spatiotopic representations become prominent after multiple saccades (Sun and Goldberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: It is unlikely that perisaccadic remapping contributed to the results of the current study.
source: The version of the double-drift illusion employed in the current study did not require saccadic eye movements, making it unlikely that perisaccadic remapping contributed to our results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design using smooth pursuit.

claim: The remapping mechanism is relevant only for saccades.
source: We find it plausible to assume, therefore, that the remapping mechanism is relevant only for saccades.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the temporal characteristics of saccades vs. smooth pursuit.

claim: A spatiotopic signal robust to smooth pursuit provides evidence for a spatiotopic representation rather than remapping.
source: Therefore, a spatiotopic signal robust to smooth pursuit provides evidence for a different correction mechanism, namely a spatiotopic representation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental design and results.

claim: The results suggest that stimulus position was encoded in a spatiotopic representation.
source: From this, our results suggest that stimulus position was encoded in a spatiotopic representation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Liu et al., 2019 used a decoding approach to identify brain activity reflecting the percept during a version of the double-drift illusion that did not include smooth pursuit.
source: A recent study Liu et al., 2019 used a decoding approach to identify brain activity reflecting the percept during a version of the double-drift illusion that did not include smooth pursuit.
evidence: This is a description of a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Liu et al. found that both veridical motion and illusory motion direction could be decoded from visual cortex.
source: Briefly, they found that both veridical motion and illusory motion direction could be decoded from visual cortex, but a classifier trained on veridical motion could not decode illusory motion and vice versa, suggesting differences between the patterns of activity in the two conditions.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a previous study.

claim: Cross-decoding between veridical and illusory motion was possible primarily in prefrontal cortex in the Liu et al. study.
source: Instead, cross-decoding was possible primarily in prefrontal cortex, suggesting that activity in PFC reflects the perceived motion direction.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a previous study.

claim: The results reported by Liu et al., 2019 are surprising because the brain regions that showed significant decoding changed when the double-drift experiment was repeated with exactly the same stimuli.
source: The results reported by Liu et al., 2019 are surprising, on several accounts. First, when the double-drift experiment was repeated with exactly the same stimuli, the brain regions that showed significant decoding changed (compare their Figure 4A with their Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of a previous study based on comparing their reported results.

claim: Multiple factors, such as spatial attention, may influence the ability to decode an illusory motion path.
source: These findings raise important questions and suggest that multiple factors, such as spatial attention, may influence the ability to decode an illusory motion path, as we have demonstrated in our study.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings and comparison with previous work.

claim: The results of Liu et al. do not have direct bearing on which reference frame was used to encode the stimulus location.
source: Regardless, the results of Liu et al. do not have direct bearing on which reference frame was used to encode the stimulus location, which is the topic of the current study.
evidence: This is an evaluative statement about the relevance of a previous study.

claim: In the Liu et al. study, the encoding of the illusion could have been in either retinal or spatiotopic coordinates because subjects were fixating on the Gabor.
source: Because in Liu et al. subjects were fixating on the Gabor, the encoding of the illusion could have been in either retinal or spatiotopic coordinates.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of a previous study.

claim: In the current study, the stimulus must have been encoded in spatiotopic coordinates.
source: In contrast, in our study, the stimulus must have been encoded in spatiotopic coordinates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental design using smooth pursuit.

claim: Data were acquired from 19 healthy participants with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: Data were acquired from 19 healthy participants (11 females, age range 23–34 y, mean 25.8 y) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant sample.

claim: The Gabor pattern consisted of a vertically oriented sinusoidal grating with spatial frequency of 1 cycle/° within a Gaussian envelope with standard deviation of 1 dva.
source: A Gabor pattern, consisting of a vertically oriented sinusoidal grating (spatial frequency of 1 cycle/°) within a Gaussian envelope (standard deviation of 1 dva), moved back and forth along a linear, vertical trajectory with a length of 8°.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus parameters.

claim: The Gabor moved according to a linear velocity profile of 10°/s.
source: The Gabor moved according to a linear velocity profile (10°/s) that was smoothed slightly at the top and bottom of the Gabor's path where it changed direction to facilitate accurate pursuit eye movements.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus motion parameters.

claim: The Gabor's internal grating moved orthogonally relative to its trajectory with a speed of 6.66 Hz.
source: The Gabor's internal grating moved orthogonally relative to its trajectory with a speed of 6.66 Hz, reversing its direction at the two endpoints of the trajectory.
evidence: This is a direct description of the internal motion parameters.

claim: Participants fixated a target positioned 9–12 dva to the left of the Gabor envelope that moved smoothly alongside it.
source: Participants fixated a target (0.2 dva, white dot with a black outer rim) that was positioned 9–12 dva to the left of the Gabor envelope and moved smoothly alongside it.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Pursuit accuracy was confirmed during the behavioral experiment for each subject prior to the fMRI experiment.
source: Pursuit accuracy was confirmed during the behavioral experiment for each subject prior to the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The Gabor completed eight traversals per block in the main fMRI experiment.
source: Each Gabor traversal lasted for 1.5 s (750 ms up, 750 ms down). The Gabor completed eight traversals in a 12 s block.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed the attend-to-stimulus task with nearly 100% accuracy.
source: The double-drift illusion is typically strong and unambiguous, even during smooth pursuit eye movements. Accordingly, participants performed the attend-to-stimulus task with nearly 100% accuracy.
evidence: This is a statement about behavioral performance in the experiment.

claim: Subjects detected the luminance changes with greater than 90% accuracy inside the scanner.
source: We found that subjects behavior improved inside the scanner and detected the luminance changes with greater than 90% accuracy.
evidence: This is a statement about behavioral performance in Experiment 2.

claim: fMRI data were acquired on a research-dedicated Siemens 7T Magnetom scanner using a 32-channel head coil.
source: fMRI data were acquired from participants on a research-dedicated Siemens 7T Magnetom scanner using a 32-channel head coil, located in the Clinical Research Center on the National Institutes of Health campus (Bethesda, MD).
evidence: This is a direct description of the scanning equipment and parameters.

claim: ROIs were defined according to an anatomical template.
source: ROIs were defined according to an anatomical template (Benson and Winawer, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis method with citation.

claim: V1, V2, and V3 were combined to form an early visual cortex ROI (EVC).
source: V1, V2, and V3 were combined to form an early visual cortex ROI (EVC)
evidence: This is a direct statement about how ROIs were defined.

claim: TO1 and TO2 were combined to form hMT+, corresponding to MT and MST.
source: TO1 and TO2 were combined to form hMT+, corresponding to MT and MST.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how ROIs were defined.

claim: Only voxels with a GLM R2 in the top 50th percentile were included in the decoding analysis.
source: We only included voxels with a GLM R2 in the top 50th percentile.
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis method.

claim: Decoding was performed with a maximum likelihood classifier using leave-one-run out cross-validation.
source: Decoding was performed with a maximum likelihood classifier using the MATLAB function 'classify' with the option 'diagLinear' (Roth et al., 2018). Decoding accuracy was computed using leave-one-run out cross-validation.
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis method with citation.

claim: A non-parametric permutation test was used to evaluate the significance of decoding accuracy.
source: A non-parametric permutation test was used to evaluate the significance of this decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis method.

claim: Accuracies were considered statistically significant when decoding accuracy was higher than the 95th percentile of the null distribution.
source: Accuracies computed using the unrandomized training data were then considered statistically significant when decoding accuracy was higher than the 95th percentile of the null distribution (p<0.05, one-tailed permutation test).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical threshold used.
